summary: This memo analyzes the X.25 packet-network interface and points out problems in its conceptual model, especially the clash between its interface role and end-to-end service. It also touches on security and implementation issues. Originally a MITRE Corporation report, it is a critique, not a specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Someone looks at a mail-sorting system and shows where its rules do not fit together well, like a mailbox that also tries to deliver the letter itself.

subtitle: Identifying fundamental design flaws in a widely adopted network interface.

tldr.problem: X.25, widely adopted as an international standard for network interfaces, has fundamental design flaws in its conceptual model and suffers from confusion about its own purpose.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes X.25's problems including ambiguous treatment of virtual circuits, end-to-end features that violate layering principles, security limitations, and inefficiencies in space and time.
tldr.outcome: This critique was influential in shaping discussions about network protocol design principles, though X.25 remained in use in many operational networks despite these identified shortcomings.

today: RFC 874 remains an important historical analysis of X.25. Despite the identified flaws, X.25 remained in operational use in many networks for years, particularly in wide-area network services offered by telecommunications carriers. The RFC contributed to ongoing debates about protocol design principles and the tension between international standards and specialized operational requirements.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 874 is a critique of the X.25 protocol and its adoption into the International Standards Organization's Open System Interconnection (ISORM) reference model as layers 1 through 3. The author, from MITRE Corporation, argues that despite X.25's widespread adoption and endorsement by standards bodies, it contains significant conceptual and practical flaws that make it unsuitable as the foundation for DoD networks.

The RFC does not propose alternatives but instead aims to expose the protocol's weaknesses before the Department of Defense commits to it as a standard. The analysis focuses on design principles, security, and implementation efficiency.
sections.plainLanguage: A famous rule book for networks (X.25) is being pushed as the best choice, but this paper shows why it is badly designed.

sections.title: Conceptual Model Problems
sections.content:
X.25 suffers from ambiguity in its core conceptual model. Advocates disagree on whether the protocol represents an end-to-end connection between hosts, a link-by-link interface between a host and a network node, or a hop-by-hop approach when networks are interconnected. This ambiguity leads to different vendor implementations that cannot interoperate correctly.

A critical flaw is X.25's treatment of the virtual circuit metaphor. When any single link fails, the entire virtual circuit is broken, and all higher-level protocols must reconstruct their own connections. This defeats a key advantage of packet switching and burdens upper layers with functionality that should be handled at the network level.

The protocol also fails to address how X.25 implementations should integrate with operating systems, particularly for out-of-band signaling—communication outside the normal data flow needed when exceptional conditions arise.
sections.plainLanguage: X.25 cannot decide what job it is supposed to do. Sometimes it acts like it is connecting two computers end-to-end, sometimes like it is just plugging one computer into the network. Also, when one connection breaks, the whole thing breaks instead of finding another route, which is bad design.

sections.title: Personality Problems and Layering Violations
sections.content:
X.25 exhibits a split personality by attempting to serve multiple roles simultaneously. It includes end-to-end features—such as DTE-to-DTE flow control, interrupt procedures, and call user data—that should not be present in a network interface protocol. These features consume memory and CPU cycles without adding value to the interface role.

Examples of superfluous mechanisms include flow control between the host and the network node (the DTE-DTE mechanism), interrupt procedures that involve the remote host, and a Q bit whose meaning violates layering by requiring higher-level protocols (like X.29) to depend on it. The absence of a proper datagram mode—where messages can be sent without delivery confirmation or flow control—suggests the designers were confused about what higher-level protocols need from a network interface.

Some advocates even propose using X.25 as a Host-Front End Protocol, a distributed processing mechanism for off-loading protocol interpretation to outboard processors. Yet the protocol lacks any explicit mechanism to support this role, forcing implementations to improvise.
sections.plainLanguage: X.25 tries to be three different things at once, like a hammer that is also a wrench and also a saw. This makes it big and slow and hard to use properly.

sections.title: Security and Space-Time Concerns
sections.content:
X.25 presents security risks. The field sizes and structure are not compatible with encryption devices commonly used to secure data. An encrypted transmission must wrap around the entire X.25 layer, meaning even the network nodes cannot read certain parts of the message—a requirement X.25 does not explicitly support. This makes deployment in secure military networks problematic.

On efficiency, X.25's design inflates the size of protocol implementations because it includes unnecessary end-to-end features. The virtual circuit model also creates delays and overhead unsuitable for applications like packetized speech, which prioritize prompt delivery over ordered delivery. The RFC notes that X.25's protocol interpreters will likely be larger and slower than they need to be because of design bloat.

Furthermore, X.25 dictates a single means of attaching a host to the network (specific electrical interfaces), which is inappropriate for diverse communication media such as satellite channels, packet radio, or local area networks where different physical interfaces might be preferred.
sections.plainLanguage: X.25 is hard to encrypt safely, and it wastes time and memory because it does too much. It also forces you to use one particular type of wire, even when other wires would work better.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.content:
The RFC concludes bluntly: X.25 is not good design. While the document presents no alternative protocol, it argues that X.25 fails on multiple grounds—conceptual clarity, proper layering, security, implementation efficiency, and flexibility. The author contends that the DoD should not adopt a protocol suite based on X.25 despite pressure from standards bodies and the claim that it represents international consensus.

The RFC notes that DoD representatives cannot fully present security concerns to the ISO process due to classification restrictions, leaving the protocol process incomplete. The fundamental issue is that X.25 was designed by telephone companies (PTTs) for a different use case than the end-to-end, resource-sharing networks the DoD requires.
sections.plainLanguage: X.25 does not work well for what the DoD needs, even though many other people like it. The design is confused, it is slow, and it does not keep information safe. The DoD should use something better.
